orig_sentences: What holds for creation, looked upon as one of the possible attitudes for the man conscious of the absurd, holds for all the styles of life open to him.
The conqueror or the actor, the creator or Don Juan may forget that their exercise in living could not do without awareness of its mad character.
One becomes accustomed so quickly.
A man wants to earn money in order to be happy, and his whole effort and the best of a life are devoted to the earning of that money.
Happiness is forgotten; the means are taken for the end.
Likewise, the whole effort of this conqueror will be diverted to ambition, which was but a way toward a greater life.
Don Juan in turn will likewise yield to his fate, be satisfied with that existence whose nobility is of value only through revolt.
For one it is awareness and for the other, revolt; in both cases the absurd has disappeared.
There is so much stubborn hope in the human heart.
The most destitute men often end up by accepting illusion.
That approval prompted by the need for peace inwardly parallels the existential consent.
There are thus gods of light and idols of mud.
But it is essential to find the middle path leading to the faces of man.
mod_sentences: Whatever holds true for artistic creation—regarded as one possible posture for the lucid individual—applies equally to every style of life open to him.
The conqueror, the actor, the artist, or Don Juan can easily forget that their way of living is meaningless without constant awareness of its absurd character.
Habit dulls the mind so rapidly.
A man sets out to earn money solely to achieve happiness, yet he pours his entire energy and the finest years of his life into accumulating that wealth.
Happiness itself is forgotten; the mere means is mistaken for the ultimate end.
In the same manner, the conqueror's entire striving becomes deflected into raw political ambition, which was originally only a stepping-stone toward a broader existence.
Don Juan, too, eventually succumbs to his fate, growing complacent with an existence whose true nobility derived exclusively from relentless defiance.
One loses lucid awareness, the other surrenders revolt; in both cases, the absurd evaporates.
Hope clings with obstinate tenacity to the human heart.
Even the most destitute men often end by embracing comforting illusions.
That inward surrender, born of the craving for peace of mind, mirrors the existential leap of faith.
Hence men erect luminous gods of light or bow before crude idols of clay.
Yet our duty is to preserve the middle road that leads directly to the living reality of human faces.
pairs.move: The creeping corruption of habit and hope. Camus warns that even absurd heroes (the conqueror, Don Juan) easily fall prey to mechanical habit, mistaking means for ends and relapsing into comforting illusions.

orig_sentences: So far, the failures of the absurd exigence have best informed us as to what it is.
In the same way, if we are to be informed, it will suffice to notice that fictional creation can present the same ambiguity as certain philosophies.
Hence I can choose as illustration a work comprising everything that denotes awareness of the absurd, having a clear starting-point and a lucid climate.
Its consequences will enlighten us.
If the absurd is not respected in it, we shall know by what expedient illusion enters in.
A particular example, a theme, a creator’s fidelity will suffice, then.
This involves the same analysis that has already been made at greater length.
mod_sentences: Until now, the breakdowns and compromises of absurd thought have best revealed its true nature to us.
Similarly, to understand absurd art, it is enough to recognize that fiction exhibits the exact same philosophical ambiguity as certain existential doctrines.
I can therefore select as a case study a literary work possessing every hallmark of absurd awareness, beginning with crystal clarity and unfolding in an atmosphere of radical lucidity.
Tracing its consequences will illuminate the problem.
If the requirements of the absurd are betrayed within it, we will see precisely through which backdoor illusion sneaks back in.
A single concrete example, a central theme, and an inquiry into the creator's fidelity will be sufficient.
This applies the identical critical method we have already practiced on formal philosophy.
pairs.move: The method of diagnosing intellectual defection. Just as Camus mapped the leaps of faith in Kierkegaard and Chestov, he now interrogates literature to detect where the novelist covertly reintroduces metaphysical hope.

orig_sentences: I shall examine a favorite theme of Dostoevsky.
I might just as well have studied other works.
But in this work the problem is treated directly, in the sense of nobility and emotion, as for the existential philosophies already discussed.
This parallelism serves my purpose.
mod_sentences: I will examine a recurrent obsession in the work of Fyodor Dostoevsky.
I could just as easily have explored other authors.
Yet in Dostoevsky, the problem of existential revolt is confronted head-on, with supreme emotional intensity and tragic nobility, matching the existential philosophies we have examined.
This exact parallel suits my inquiry perfectly.
pairs.move: Selecting Dostoevsky as the supreme laboratory of existential fiction. Dostoevsky directly dramatizes the boundary between radical metaphysical revolt and Christian surrender.

orig_sentences: All of Dostoevsky’s heroes question themselves as to the meaning of life.
In this they are modern: they do not fear ridicule.
What distinguishes modern sensibility from classical sensibility is that the latter thrives on moral problems and the former on metaphysical problems.
In Dostoevsky’s novels the question is propounded with such intensity that it can only invite extreme solutions.
Existence is illusory or it is eternal.
If Dostoevsky were satisfied with this inquiry, he would be a philosopher.
But he illustrates the consequences that such intellectual pastimes may have in a man’s life, and in this regard he is an artist.
Among those consequences, his attention is arrested particularly by the last one, which he himself calls logical suicide.
In his Diary of a Writer he mentions this.
It is worth while to consider the reasonings by which the logical suicide, because he is not convinced of the immortality of the soul, comes to the following conclusions:
mod_sentences: Every one of Dostoevsky’s protagonists tortures himself over the meaning of life.
In this, they are thoroughly modern: they have zero fear of looking ridiculous.
What separates modern consciousness from classical sensibility is that the classical mind wrestles with moral dilemmas, whereas the modern mind is consumed by metaphysical dread.
In Dostoevsky’s novels, the question of existence is posed with such agonizing force that it admits only radical, absolute answers.
Either existence is a meaningless phantom, or it is eternal.
Were Dostoevsky content with mere abstract inquiry, he would be simply an academic philosopher.
Instead, he dramatizes the catastrophic consequences such questions unleash within a living person's existence—and in this, he proves himself a true artist.
Among those consequences, his focus is seized above all by the most extreme outcome, which he terms 'logical suicide.'
He outlines this concept in his Diary of a Writer.
It is instructive to follow the exact reasoning by which the logical suicide—unconvinced of the soul's immortality—arrives at his final verdict:
pairs.move: Metaphysical vs. moral sensibility. Classical literature dealt with ethics; modern literature wrestles with cosmic meaning. Dostoevsky is an artist because he shows the physical, deadly consequences of ideas, particularly 'logical suicide.'

orig_sentences: “Since in reply to my questions touching upon happiness, I am told, through the medium of my consciousness, that I cannot be happy except in harmony with the great all, which I cannot conceive and shall never be in a position to conceive, it is evident …”
mod_sentences: 'Since, in reply to my questions regarding happiness, my own consciousness informs me that I cannot find peace except in harmony with the cosmic totality—a totality I cannot conceive and will never be capable of grasping—it is self-evident...'
pairs.move: The first premise of logical suicide: Human consciousness demands harmony with the universe, yet the universe remains inherently incomprehensible to mortal reason.

orig_sentences: “Since, finally, in this connection, I assume both the role of the plaintiff and that of the defendant, of the accused and of the judge, and since I find this comedy on the part of nature utterly stupid, and since I deem it humiliating on my part to accept it …

In my indisputable capacity of plaintiff and defendant, of judge and accused, I condemn that nature which, with such impudent nerve, brought me into being in order to suffer—I condemn it to be annihilated with me.”
mod_sentences: 'Since, finally, under these conditions, I find myself forced to play simultaneously the role of plaintiff and defendant, of the accused and the judge; and since I consider this cosmic charade on the part of nature utterly senseless and degrading to endure...

In my indisputable authority as plaintiff and defendant, judge and accused, I condemn that indifferent nature which, with insolent arrogance, created me solely to suffer—and I sentence it to be destroyed along with myself.'
pairs.move: The indictment of nature. The suicide acts as both prosecutor and judge, declaring that by ending his own life, he annihilates the universe that insolently generated him to suffer.

orig_sentences: There remains a little humor in that position.
This suicide kills himself because, on the metaphysical level, he is vexed.
In a certain sense he takes his revenge.
This is his way of proving that “he won’t be taken in.”
It is known, however, that the same theme is embodied, but with the most wonderful generality, in Kirilov of The Possessed, likewise an advocate of logical suicide.
Kirilov the engineer declares somewhere that he wants to take his life because “it is his idea.”
It is clear that this is a question of a proper reason.
He is preparing for death for an idea, for a thought.
It is a superior suicide.
Successively, in scenes in which Kirilov’s mask is gradually illuminated, the fatal thought inspiring him is revealed to us.
The engineer, in fact, resumes the reasonings of the Diary.
He feels that God is necessary and that he must exist.
But he knows that he does not exist and cannot exist.
“Why don’t you understand,” he exclaims, “that this is reason enough for killing oneself?”
That attitude also entails for him some of the absurd consequences.
Through indifferent generosity he accepts having his death utilized for the benefit of a cause he despises.
Stavrogin: “I began to realize this evening that you might be in earnest after all.”
Kirilov: “I am in earnest.”
Stavrogin: “Did you think of it today?”
Kirilov: “No, long ago.
Ever since I can remember, I have thought about it.”
He prepares his deed with that mixed feeling of revolt and passion.
“I want to shoot myself,” he says, “because this is my great idea, my supreme liberty.”
It is no longer a question of revenge, but of revolt.
Kirilov is, then, an absurd character—with the essential reservation, however, that he is about to die.
He himself explains that contradiction, but in such a way that he reveals at the same time the absurd secret in all its purity.
Indeed, he adds to his fatal logic an extraordinary ambition which gives the character its full perspective: he wants to kill himself to become god.
mod_sentences: There is a grim, ironical humor in this stance.
This individual takes his life because, on a cosmic level, he feels deeply insulted.
In a sense, he is exacting revenge.
It is his definitive method of proving that he will not be played for a fool.
Yet this same theme achieves its most magnificent, universal expression in Kirillov from Demons, who is likewise a practitioner of logical suicide.
Kirillov, the civil engineer, declares plainly that he intends to end his life because 'it is his idea.'
Clearly, this represents a deliberate, calculated conviction.
He prepares to die for an idea—for a pure principle of thought.
This is suicide elevated to intellectual mastery.
Step by step, through scenes where Kirillov’s internal visage is progressively unveiled, his governing obsession is laid bare.
The engineer essentially adopts the syllogisms from Dostoevsky's Diary.
He senses that God is indispensable and ought to exist.
Yet he knows with absolute certainty that God does not exist and cannot exist.
'How can you fail to understand,' he cries, 'that this alone is a sufficient reason to kill oneself?'
This radical posture produces in him several characteristic absurd behaviors.
With chilling indifference, he even allows his impending death to be exploited by a political conspiracy he completely disdains.
Stavrogin asks: 'I realized only tonight that you are genuinely serious.'
Kirillov replies: 'I am entirely serious.'
Stavrogin presses: 'Did you decide this today?'
Kirillov answers: 'No, long ago.
For as long as I can remember, I have thought of nothing else.'
He orchestrates his demise with that unique mixture of defiance and cold passion.
'I will shoot myself,' he insists, 'because it is my great idea—my supreme assertion of freedom.'
This is no longer petty personal revenge; it is metaphysical revolt.
Kirillov stands as a quintessential absurd hero—bearing, however, the fatal contradiction that he chooses physical death.
Yet he explains this apparent contradiction himself, revealing the absurd core in all its terrifying purity.
He attaches to his lethal logic a staggering metaphysical ambition that unveils the true scope of his character: he resolves to kill himself in order to become God.
pairs.move: Introducing Kirillov's 'superior suicide.' Unlike the emotional suicide driven by heartbreak or despair, Kirillov kills himself for an intellectual principle: God ought to exist, yet does not exist; therefore man must assert absolute sovereignty by choosing death.

orig_sentences: The reasoning is classic in its clarity.
If God does not exist, Kirilov is god.
If God does not exist, Kirilov must kill himself.
Kirilov must therefore kill himself to become god.
That logic is absurd, but it is what is needed.
What remains interesting, however, is to give a meaning to that divinity brought down to earth.
That amounts to clarifying the premise: “If God does not exist, I am god.”
If God exists, all depends on him and we can do nothing against his will.
If he does not exist, everything depends on us.
For Kirilov, as for Nietzsche, to kill God is to become god oneself; it is to realize on this earth the eternal life of which the Gospel speaks.
But if this metaphysical crime is enough for man’s fulfillment, why add suicide?
Why kill oneself and leave this world after having won freedom?
That is contradictory.
Kirilov is well aware of this, for he adds: “If you feel that, you are a tsar and, far from killing yourself, you will live covered with glory.”
Yet the divinity in question is completely terrestrial.
“For three years,” says Kirilov, “I sought the attribute of my divinity and I’ve found it: the attribute of my divinity is independence.”
Now can be seen the meaning of Kirilov’s premise: “If God does not exist, I am god.”
To become god is merely to be free on this earth, not to serve an immortal being.
Above all, of course, it is drawing all the painful consequences from that painful independence.
If God does not exist, we are responsible for everything.
It is to realize that our actions no longer have any supernatural guarantee.
Consequently, we must take the full weight upon our shoulders.
To give words their specific sense would, in this instance, be ridiculous.
mod_sentences: The dialectical reasoning is classical in its razor clarity.
If God does not exist, Kirillov is God.
If God does not exist, Kirillov must kill himself.
Therefore, Kirillov must take his own life in order to become God.
This logic appears paradoxical, yet it follows its premises to the bitter end.
What remains vital is deciphering what divinity means once brought down to mortal earth.
It requires unpacking Kirillov’s foundational axiom: 'If God does not exist, then I am God.'
If God exists, everything is subject to His sovereign will, and our autonomy is an illusion.
If He does not exist, then everything rests entirely upon human shoulders.
For Kirillov, exactly as for Friedrich Nietzsche, to dethrone God is to assume divinity oneself—to claim directly upon this earth the eternal sovereignty promised in religious scripture.
Yet if this metaphysical liberation suffices to fulfill human destiny, why crown it with self-destruction?
Why slaughter oneself and abandon the world the very moment absolute freedom has been conquered?
On the surface, this appears completely contradictory.
Kirillov is acutely aware of the paradox, adding: 'If you truly feel this, you are a king, and far from killing yourself, you will live cloaked in glory.'
Yet the divinity he envisions is strictly terrestrial and mortal.
'For three years,' Kirillov confesses, 'I searched for the true attribute of my divinity, and I found it: the attribute of my divinity is absolute independence.'
Here the true meaning of his declaration becomes transparent: 'If God does not exist, I am God.'
To become God simply means to live entirely autonomous on this earth, bowing before no celestial master.
Above all, it means bearing every agonizing consequence of that terrible independence.
If God does not exist, we bear solitary responsibility for the entire universe.
It means recognizing that our choices possess zero cosmic guarantees or moral safety nets.
Consequently, human beings must shoulder the full existential burden themselves.
To interpret Kirillov’s words in a traditional mystical sense would, in this context, be absurd.
pairs.move: The deconstruction of 'If God does not exist, I am God.' Divinity is unmasked not as supernatural omnipotence, but as radical mortal autonomy. Killing God means accepting total responsibility without celestial appeals or safety nets.

orig_sentences: Kirilov himself helps us to understand.
In reply to a question from Stavrogin, he specifies that he is not talking about a god-man.
One might think that this is aimed at distinguishing himself from Christ.
In reality it is a matter of annexing him.
Kirilov in fact fancies for a moment that Jesus at his death did not find himself in Paradise.
He found out then that his torture had been useless.
“The laws of nature,” says the engineer, “made Christ live in the midst of falsehood and die for a falsehood.”
Solely in this sense Jesus personifies the whole human drama.
He is the complete man, he who realized the most absurd condition.
He is not the God-man, but the man-god.
And, like him, each of us can be crucified and victimized—and is to a certain degree.
mod_sentences: Kirillov provides the key to his own paradox.
In response to Stavrogin’s probing, he clarifies that he is not speaking of a 'God-man.'
One might assume this distinction is intended to separate him from Jesus of Nazareth.
In reality, Kirillov seeks to reclaim Jesus as his brother in absurdity.
Kirillov imagines that when Christ died on the cross, he did not awake in Paradise.
He discovered at the final moment that his agonizing martyrdom had been in vain.
'The laws of nature,' the engineer asserts, 'forced Christ to live amidst illusion and to die for a lie.'
In this precise sense alone, Jesus embodies the total tragedy of the human condition.
He represents the archetypal mortal: the man who lived the absurd condition to its ultimate extremity.
He was not the divine God made man, but the mortal man striving to become God.
And like him, every conscious human being is crucified and betrayed by the indifferent silence of nature.
pairs.move: The tragic secularization of Christ. Kirillov identifies with Jesus not as a divine redeemer, but as the supreme martyr of cosmic absurdity: a mortal who died for a nonexistent heaven, discovering on the cross that nature is indifferent.

orig_sentences: But if this metaphysical crime is enough for man’s fulfillment, why add suicide?
Why kill oneself and leave this world after having won freedom?
That is contradictory.
Kirilov is well aware of this, for he adds: “If you feel that, you are a tsar and, far from killing yourself, you will live covered with glory.”
But men in general do not know it.
They do not feel “that.”
As in the time of Prometheus, they entertain blind hopes.
They need to be shown the way and cannot do without preaching.
Consequently, Kirilov must kill himself out of love for humanity.
He must show his brothers a royal and difficult path on which he will be the first.
It is a pedagogical suicide.
Kirilov sacrifices himself, then.
But if he is crucified, he will not be victimized.
He remains the man-god, convinced of a death without future, imbued with evangelical melancholy.
“I,” he says, “am unhappy because I am obliged to assert my freedom.”
Kirilov’s pistol shot will be the signal for the last revolution.
Thus, it is not despair that urges him to death, but love of his neighbor for his own sake.
Before terminating in blood an indescribable spiritual adventure, Kirilov makes a remark as old as human suffering: “All is well.”
mod_sentences: Yet if overthrowing God is sufficient for human dignity, why crown it with a bullet to the brain?
Why take one's own life and abandon existence the very instant absolute liberation has been won?
The act seems glaringly contradictory.
Kirillov recognizes this perfectly, noting: 'If you comprehend this truth, you become a sovereign king, and rather than killing yourself, you will live cloaked in splendor.'
Yet ordinary humanity remains blind to this insight.
Mankind does not grasp 'that.'
Exactly as in the myth of Prometheus, human beings cling desperately to blind, metaphysical hopes.
They require a visible prophet to show them the path, unable to awaken without an undeniable demonstration.
Therefore, Kirillov resolves to kill himself out of pure, selfless love for mankind.
He must demonstrate to his fellow men a sovereign, terrifying path on which he will be the first pioneer.
His death is a pedagogical suicide.
Kirillov offers himself as a sacrificial vanguard.
Yet though he goes to his own cross, he refuses to play the helpless victim.
He remains the 'man-god,' lucidly assured that death is total annihilation, yet steeped in tragic, evangelical compassion.
'I am wretched,' he laments, 'because I am bound by duty to proclaim my absolute freedom.'
Kirillov’s gunshot is designed as the starting bell for the final human revolution—the liberation from cosmic terror.
Thus, it is not despair or misery that drives him to self-destruction, but an overflowing love for his fellow mortals.
And before ending this extraordinary spiritual drama in a puddle of blood, Kirillov utters words as ancient as human suffering: 'All is well.'
pairs.move: Pedagogical suicide: Kirillov kills himself not from despair, but as a secular savior. To liberate humanity from the ancient terror of death and the phantom of God, he must sacrifice himself to prove that man is the sole master of his destiny.

orig_sentences: This theme of suicide in Dostoevsky, then, is indeed an absurd theme.
Let us merely note before going on that Kirilov reappears in other characters who themselves set in motion additional absurd themes.
Stavrogin and Ivan Karamazov try out the absurd truths in practical life.
They are the ones liberated by Kirilov’s death.
They try their skill at being tsars.
Stavrogin leads an “ironic” life, and it is well known in what regard.
He arouses hatred around him.
And yet the key to the character is found in his farewell letter: “I have not been able to detest anything.”
He is a tsar in indifference.
Ivan is likewise by refusing to surrender the royal powers of the mind.
To those who, like his brother, prove by their lives that it is essential to humiliate oneself in order to believe, he might reply that the condition is shameful.
His key word is: “Everything is permitted,” with the appropriate shade of melancholy.
Of course, like Nietzsche, the most famous of God’s assassins, he ends in madness.
But this is a risk worth running, and, faced with such tragic ends, the essential impulse of the absurd mind is to ask: “What does that prove?”
They establish logic unto death, exaltation, “dreadful” freedom, the glory of the tsars become human.
All is well, everything is permitted, and nothing is hateful—these are absurd judgments.
But what an amazing creation in which those creatures of fire and ice seem so familiar to us.
The passionate world of indifference that rumbles in their hearts does not seem at all monstrous to us.
We recognize in it our everyday anxieties.
mod_sentences: Suicide in Dostoevsky’s universe is therefore an undeniably absurd theme.
Before advancing, we must observe that Kirillov’s metaphysical rebellion reemerges in other characters who embody related absurd postures.
Nikolai Stavrogin and Ivan Karamazov attempt to live out these absurd realizations in concrete action.
They represent those who have been theoretically liberated by Kirillov’s sacrifice.
They test their prowess at reigning as sovereign kings of their own lives.
Stavrogin lives an existence of cold, corrosive irony—and its destructive fallout is infamous.
He incites intense hatred everywhere he walks.
Yet the definitive cipher to his soul appears in his final suicide note: 'I have never been capable of hating anything.'
He is a sovereign king of pure indifference.
Ivan Karamazov claims identical kingship by adamantly refusing to surrender the intellectual sovereignty of reason.
To those who, like his saintly brother Alyosha, argue that one must humiliate human reason to accept faith, Ivan retorts that such spiritual surrender is shameful.
His defining motto remains 'Everything is permitted'—tinged with an unmistakable undercurrent of melancholy.
Inevitably, like Nietzsche—the most famous assassin of God—Ivan collapses into madness.
Yet this is an occupational hazard of radical honesty, and confronted with such tragic ruins, the absurd mind simply asks: 'What does that prove?'
Dostoevsky’s novels construct a ruthless logic pursued to the point of death: ecstasy, terrifying freedom, and the tragic majesty of mortals crowned as kings.
'All is well,' 'Everything is permitted,' and 'I can hate nothing'—these are quintessential absurd verdicts.
Yet what a breathtaking imaginative triumph it is that these characters of fire and ice feel so intimately recognizable to us.
The stormy universe of indifference churning within their breasts does not strike us as alien or monstrous.
We recognize within their torment the magnified reflection of our own daily anxieties.
pairs.move: The absurd triumvirate: Kirillov (suicide to prove freedom), Stavrogin (sovereign indifference), and Ivan Karamazov ('Everything is permitted'). Their tragic ends (madness, suicide) do not refute their logic; they confirm the terrifying weight of lucidity.

orig_sentences: Yet what is his conclusion?
Two quotations will show the complete metaphysical reversal that leads the writer to other revelations.

The argument of the one who commits logical suicide having provoked protests from the critics, Dostoevsky in the following installments of the Diary amplifies his position and concludes thus: “If faith in immortality is so necessary to the human being (that without it he comes to the point of killing himself), it must therefore be the normal state of humanity.
Since this is the case, the immortality of the human soul exists without any doubt.”

Then again in the last pages of his last novel, at the conclusion of that gigantic combat with God, some children ask Aliocha: “Karamazov, is it true what religion says, that we shall rise from the dead, that we shall see one another again?”
And Aliocha answers: “Certainly, we shall see one another again, we shall joyfully tell one another everything that has happened.”
mod_sentences: Yet where does Dostoevsky himself ultimately land?
Two passages reveal the total metaphysical reversal through which the novelist retreats toward transcendent consolation.

When his essay on logical suicide provoked furious outrage from contemporary critics, Dostoevsky clarified his stance in subsequent issues of the Diary, deducing: 'If faith in eternal life is so indispensable to human sanity that without it man is driven to destroy himself, then immortality must represent the natural, intended state of humanity.'
'Because this need is universal, the immortality of the human soul must exist beyond any shadow of a doubt.'

And again, in the closing chapter of his final masterpiece, at the climax of that monumental wrestling match with God, schoolboys gather around Alyosha asking: 'Karamazov, is it true what faith teaches—that we will rise from the dead, that we will see each other again?'
And Alyosha reassures them: 'Without question, we will see each other again, and we will joyfully recount everything that has happened.'
pairs.move: The author's philosophical retreat. Camus exposes Dostoevsky's intellectual leap of faith: arguing that because man cannot endure mortality without despair, immortality MUST exist (the pragmatic fallacy), culminating in Alyosha's promise of resurrection.

orig_sentences: Thus Kirilov, Stavrogin, and Ivan are defeated.
The Brothers Karamazov replies to The Possessed.
And it is indeed a conclusion.
Aliocha’s case is not ambiguous, as is that of Prince Muichkin.
Ill, the latter lives in a perpetual present, tinged with smiles and indifference, and that blissful state might be the eternal life of which the Prince speaks.
On the contrary, Aliocha clearly says: “We shall meet again.”
There is no longer any question of suicide and of madness.
What is the use, for anyone who is sure of immortality and of its joys?
Man exchanges his divinity for happiness.
“We shall joyfully tell one another everything that has happened.”
Thus again Kirilov’s pistol rang out somewhere in Russia, but the world continued to cherish its blind hopes.
Men did not understand “that.”
Consequently, it is not an absurd novelist addressing us, but an existential novelist.
Here, too, the leap is touching and gives its nobility to the art that inspires it.
It is a stirring acquiescence, riddled with doubts, uncertain and ardent.

Speaking of The Brothers Karamazov, Dostoevsky wrote: “The chief question that will be pursued throughout this book is the very one from which I have suffered consciously or unconsciously all life long: the existence of God.”
It is hard to believe that a novel sufficed to transform into joyful certainty the suffering of a lifetime.

One commentator correctly pointed out that Dostoevsky is on Ivan’s side and that the affirmative chapters took three months of effort whereas what he called “the blasphemies” were written in three weeks in a state of excitement.
There is not one of his characters who does not have that thorn in the flesh, who does not aggravate it or seek a remedy for it in sensation or immortality.
In any case, let us remain with this doubt.
Here is a work which, in a chiaroscuro more gripping than the light of day, permits us to seize man’s struggle against his hopes.
Having reached the end, the creator makes his choice against his characters.
That contradiction thus allows us to make a distinction.
It is not an absurd work that is involved here, but a work that propounds the absurd problem.
mod_sentences: Thus Kirillov, Stavrogin, and Ivan Karamazov are ultimately repudiated by their creator.
The Brothers Karamazov is written as an explicit refutation of Demons.
And it represents a definitive theological verdict.
Alyosha’s spiritual certainty contains none of Prince Myshkin’s holy ambiguity.
The epileptic Myshkin inhabits a perpetual present bathed in luminous indifference—a state that closely mirrors the terrestrial eternal life of which the Gospel speaks.
Alyosha, by contrast, proclaims without hesitation: 'We will meet again.'
Suicide and existential madness are banished from the horizon.
For what reason would anyone take their own life if they are guaranteed the everlasting bliss of heaven?
Man abdicates his tragic divinity in exchange for celestial security.
'We will joyfully recount everything that has happened.'
Once more, Kirillov’s pistol echoed through the Russian night, but the world moved on, nursing its stubborn illusions.
Mankind failed to comprehend his sacrifice.
Therefore, the writer speaking to us is not an absurd creator, but an existential novelist who executes a leap of faith.
Yet here too, the leap is deeply moving, lending tragic nobility to the literature born from it.
It is an agonizing surrender, besieged by skepticism, trembling and feverish.

Reflecting upon The Brothers Karamazov, Dostoevsky admitted: 'The central question running through every page of this novel is the identical torment that has haunted my conscience all my life: the existence of God.'
It is difficult to believe that the pages of a novel could magically transform the lifelong anguish of a titan into serene religious faith.

A perceptive critic rightly observed that Dostoevsky's instinctive sympathy lay with Ivan: the pious refutations required three months of agonizing labor, whereas the fiery 'blasphemies' were drafted in three weeks of incandescent inspiration.
Every single one of his characters carries that agonizing thorn in the flesh, inflaming the wound or seeking an antidote through sensory excess or dreams of eternity.
Regardless, let us honor the unresolved tension of his struggle.
We are left with a masterpiece whose chiaroscuro—more haunting than midday sun—captures the desperate combat between man and his own craving for hope.
Arriving at the final crossroads, the creator sides against his own greatest creations.
That crucial betrayal allows us to establish a vital aesthetic distinction.
Dostoevsky's fiction is not an absurd work; it is a work that powerfully dramatizes the absurd problem only to flee from its conclusion.
pairs.move: The creator choosing against his characters. Dostoevsky's emotional genius was on the side of Ivan's blasphemies, but his theological terror forced a Christian resolution. It is a work that poses the absurd question with genius, but resolves it through an existential leap.

orig_sentences: Dostoevsky’s reply is humiliation, “shame” according to Stavrogin.
An absurd work, on the contrary, does not provide a reply; that is the whole difference.
Let us note this carefully in conclusion: what contradicts the absurd in that work is not its Christian character, but rather its announcing a future life.
It is possible to be Christian and absurd.
There are examples of Christians who do not believe in a future life.
In regard to the work of art, it should therefore be possible to define one of the directions of the absurd analysis that could have been anticipated in the preceding pages.
It leads to propounding “the absurdity of the Gospel.”
It throws light upon this idea, fertile in repercussions, that convictions do not prevent incredulity.
On the contrary, it is easy to see that the author of The Possessed, familiar with these paths, in conclusion took a quite different way.
The surprising reply of the creator to his characters, of Dostoevsky to Kirilov, can indeed be summed up thus: existence is illusory and it is eternal.
mod_sentences: Dostoevsky’s final answer is holy humiliation—what Stavrogin calls 'shame.'
An authentically absurd creation, by contrast, offers zero consoling answers; that is the absolute divide.
We must emphasize this carefully: what betrays the absurd in Dostoevsky’s work is not that it is Christian, but that it promises an afterlife.
It is entirely possible to be Christian and remain faithful to the absurd.
History offers instances of Christians who harbored no belief in personal immortality.
With respect to aesthetics, one could explore a radical direction of absurd analysis hinted at in the preceding chapters.
It would explore 'the absurdity of the Gospel' itself.
It illuminates the profound insight that intense religious longing does not preclude radical skepticism.
Yet the author of Demons, though intimately acquainted with these precipices, chose an entirely different escape route in the end.
The startling answer the creator offers his characters—the reply Dostoevsky delivers to Kirillov—can be distilled into a single formula: existence is an illusion, and it is eternal.
pairs.move: The decisive aesthetic verdict: Absurd art provides no answers. Dostoevsky's betrayal of the absurd is not his Christianity, but his promise of an afterlife. He reconciles the world by declaring existence both illusory and eternal.
